name: Cast in bronze, fettled and chased
process: The bronze is poured into a lost-wax (investment) or sand mould. When cold, the mould is broken away and the casting is fettled: sprues, runners and vents are cut off and ground back. It is then chased: flaws and fins are removed and the detail re-cut with chasing tools and files. Finally the skin is cleaned by a fine abrasive blast, which leaves an even, non-directional matte of bright metal, and the piece is waxed. This is the bronze as the founder hands it over before any colour is given: a warm golden metal with a soft, grainy lustre.

steps.text: As-fabricated castings carry the mould's own surface: 'as-cast surfaces will betray the nature of the foundry method employed'. The CDA/NAAMM designation of an as-cast matte is M12.
steps.source: Copper Development Association, 'Copper Brass Bronze Design Handbook: Architectural Applications' (A4039), Table 16 (M12 'Matte finish as fabricated: ... casting') and p. 38, https://www.copper.org/publications/pub_list/pdf/A4039-ArchitecturalApplications.pdf

steps.text: The shell is hammered or blasted away, the sprues are cut off, and the casting is chased: 'worked until the telltale signs of the casting process are removed, so that the casting now looks like the original model'; pits from air bubbles and the stubs of the sprues are filed down.
steps.source: Wikipedia, 'Lost-wax casting', steps Release and Metal-chasing, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lost-wax_casting

steps.text: CDA/NAAMM M42 fine matte: air blast with #100-#200 mesh silica sand or aluminium oxide, gun 305 mm from the work at 60-90 degrees. 'The process is often used to clean castings and improve appearance of an as-cast surface.'

abrasiveMesh.source: Copper Development Association, A4039, Table 16 (M42 Fine matte), https://www.copper.org/publications/pub_list/pdf/A4039-ArchitecturalApplications.pdf

airPressure.source: Copper Development Association, A4039, Table 16 (M42: 30-90 psi (207-621 kPa)), https://www.copper.org/publications/pub_list/pdf/A4039-ArchitecturalApplications.pdf

gunDistance.source: Copper Development Association, A4039, Table 16 (M42: 'Gun 12 in (305 mm) away from work'), https://www.copper.org/publications/pub_list/pdf/A4039-ArchitecturalApplications.pdf

gunAngle.source: Copper Development Association, A4039, Table 16 (M42: 'at an angle of 60-90 degrees'), https://www.copper.org/publications/pub_list/pdf/A4039-ArchitecturalApplications.pdf

steps.text: Blasted surfaces hold oils and dirt and show fingerprints; for an untarnished finish they need a protective treatment. Wax (or oil) is the founder's protection for statuary finishes and is renewed by hand-rubbing.
steps.source: Copper Development Association, A4039, p. 40 ('Even fine-grit blasted surfaces are rough enough to retain oils and dirt, and will show fingerprints. For an untarnished finish, sand blasted surfaces require protective treatment') and p. 42 ('hand-rubbed periodically with wax or oils'), https://www.copper.org/publications/pub_list/pdf/A4039-ArchitecturalApplications.pdf

surface.texture: non-directional matte from the blast, over the chased form
surface.metal: bare: the substance's own conductor optics (bronze f0) with no dielectric layer except a thin wax film
surface.note: Roughness has no verified measurement for blasted bronze (see unverified). The texture is isotropic.

photograph: An even, fine, non-directional matte of golden metal over crisp chased detail; no scratch direction.
Fingerprints show as darker smudges on the matte.

unverified.reason: No measured Ra for M42-blasted or investment-cast copper alloy was read; the Degarmo et al. chart cited by Wikipedia ('Surface finish') could not be read as text.
No measured thickness or refractive index for a microcrystalline wax film on bronze was read.
